claim: The tone controls these two types carry are one pair of first-order shelves whose corners are fixed and have no byte: a low shelf at 161 Hz and a high shelf at or above 5187 Hz. The pair is the same pair on both types -- fitted to each type on its own the low corners land 0.0 octaves apart and the high ones 0.0119, and one shared pair scores each record as well as its own fit does. The section is one pole and one zero: a unit-slope second-order shelf is two to three times worse on the median of every one of the four records and three times worse at its worst, and its worst band is in the shelf's own transition every time. The gain is not fitted here at all -- it is the window the gain class closed on, twenty-five values centred on 64 that stick at both ends, and the same window that type 01 00 was read with.
named: a fixed first-order shelf pair, the part's tone control
adds: The records say what each gain byte did to each band at four settings of the low control and two of the high, on two types. What is read out of them here is that those profiles are shelves, that the shelves are one pole and one zero rather than a pair, where the corners are, and that the two types' corners are the same corners. The records name no filter, no corner and no order, and say so.
refutedBy: A tone control on a third type whose corners are not these, which would make the pair the type's rather than the part's. Or either shelf read with a band set reaching past where it settles and coming back at twelve decibels an octave.

eraPriors.claim: A tone control with no corner byte is a section written once with its coefficients compiled in, reached by whichever type wants one.
eraPriors.why: A corner nobody can set needs no table and no runtime arithmetic, so the cheap thing is one routine with two constants in it. Two types built at different times would have no reason to land on the same two constants.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: A third type's tone controls came back on a different pair of corners, which would make the pair the type's and not the part's.

alternatives.reading: A unit-slope second-order shelf, which is the shelf a part that already has biquads gets for free.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Its worst band is in the shelf's own transition on all four records -- 6.2 to 6.6 decibels out where the first-order pair is 2.0 to 2.4 -- and it has to move the corner to get there: fitted on its own it puts the low shelf at 291 Hz against 161 and the high at 3.2 kHz against 5.2, and is still twice as far out. A slope twice as steep cannot be hidden in a corner.

alternatives.reading: The pair is shared because the two types call one routine, rather than because two routines were given the same two constants.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: Not applicable: the two readings differ in where the code is and in nothing that comes out of it.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: The same shape recorded twice in the same archive. What the agreement does rule out is two *different* pairs, which is the thing that was worth asking: corners fitted to each type separately land 0.0 and 0.0119 octaves apart, under what either band set resolves.

The second-order pair's worst band is inside the shelf's transition on every record -- 167 Hz for a shelf it puts at 291, 5.3 kHz for one it puts at 3.2 -- which is a slope in the wrong place rather than a fit that is slightly worse. figures.read_as: It returns structure on all four and the reason is different on the two controls, so neither is read as the model breaking down. On the low control the swing is between 25 Hz and 59 Hz, where this run's own repeats of one setting spread 0.31 and 1.11 decibels against 0.05 above 100 -- the signed median alternates sign across those bands rather than running one way. On the high control the swing is at 6 kHz, and both records say there why: the deviation was still climbing where the band set ended, so the corner is the lowest one consistent with the readings and a lean up there is that bound leaning. The scoring carries the record's own figure for this and it reads as a bound on 01 50 by that figure. The verdict is left as it came back.

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// roland-sc8850-01  ·  filter-section
//
// Generated by yarn sync from inferences/models/tone-a-fixed-shelf-pair-order-1.json.
// The claim it closes: inferences/roland-sc8850-01/tone-a-pair-of-fixed-first-order-shelves.json
//
// Every constant, every section count and every structural choice below is
// the model's. The difference equations are the ordinary realisations of the
// sections the model names — this site's arithmetic, not a measurement.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#include <cmath>

namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::filter_section {

// Carried from the classes that measured it rather than fitted here. A shelf this far
// below half the rate is its analogue self whichever of the candidate rates is used, so
// this record cannot and need not say.
constexpr double kSampleRateHz = 32000.0;
constexpr double kPi = 3.14159265358979323846;

/**
 * A first-order shelf: one pole, one zero, tilting the two sides of its corner
 * against each other. `(s + w0 * V) / (s + w0)` for a low shelf and
 * `(V * s + w0) / (s + w0)` for a high one, bilinear-transformed.
 */
struct Shelf1 {
  enum class Side { Low, High };

  double b0 = 1.0, b1 = 0.0, a1 = 0.0, x1 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0;

  void set(double hz, double gainDb, Side side) {
    const double v = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 20.0);
    const double k = std::tan(kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
    const double norm = 1.0 / (1.0 + k);
    a1 = (k - 1.0) * norm;
    if (side == Side::Low) {
      b0 = (1.0 + v * k) * norm;
      b1 = (v * k - 1.0) * norm;
    } else {
      b0 = (v + k) * norm;
      b1 = (k - v) * norm;
    }
  }

  double process(double x) {
    const double y = b0 * x + b1 * x1 - a1 * y1;
    x1 = x;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

// a ramp from -12 at 52 to 12 at 76, holding both ends
// read from data/units/roland-sc8850-01/efx-bands/01-00-04-how-much-is-twelve-db-fine-in-twelfths.json
inline double shelf0GainDb(int byte) {
  if (byte <= 52) return -12.0;
  if (byte >= 76) return 12.0;
  const double t = (byte - 52) / 24.0;
  return -12.0 + t * 24.0;
}

// a ramp from -12 at 52 to 12 at 76, holding both ends
// read from data/units/roland-sc8850-01/efx-bands/01-00-04-how-much-is-twelve-db-fine-in-twelfths.json
inline double shelf1GainDb(int byte) {
  if (byte <= 52) return -12.0;
  if (byte >= 76) return 12.0;
  const double t = (byte - 52) / 24.0;
  return -12.0 + t * 24.0;
}

/** The chain the model names, in the order it names it. */
struct Effect {
  Shelf1 shelf0;
  Shelf1 shelf1;

  void prepare(int b40_03_13, int b40_03_14) {
    shelf0.set(160.596898725, shelf0GainDb(b40_03_13), Shelf1::Side::Low);
    shelf1.set(5187.16499104, shelf1GainDb(b40_03_14), Shelf1::Side::High);
  }

  double process(double x) {
    x = shelf0.process(x);
    x = shelf1.process(x);
    return x;
  }
};
